one_liner: Fernleaf wants its runway model and pricing plan pressure-tested so it can make two decisions before a Q2 2027 Series A.
background: Fernleaf sells weekly bread and pastry subscriptions for 310 independent bakeries, 22 months after launch. It raised a $1.2M seed round 11 months ago and has a team of 7. It plans to raise a Series A in Q2 2027 and does not want a bridge round.
goals: Leave with a runway model the founders can defend in front of Series A investors.
Decide whether to hire two engineers now or after passing $600k ARR.
Know how to model the effect of a $79 to $129 price increase on churn and payback.
Pick the unit economics to lead with in the Series A deck.
key_facts: $420k ARR, growing about 6% month over month for two quarters.
Gross margin about 78%; blended CAC about $640 per bakery.
Net burn about $85k per month; $1.19M cash as of October 1.
Two more engineers would add about $32k per month fully loaded.
Multi-location support ships in December; the largest customers say they would pay more for it.
Board update with a hiring plan due to the lead seed investor by November 20.
questions: What will Series A investors look at first in the runway model?
Should Fernleaf hire two engineers now or wait until $600k ARR?
How should the price increase be modelled for churn and payback?
Which unit economics should lead the Series A deck?
gaps: The runway spreadsheet is attached separately and isn't in this brief.
No cohort or net revenue retention data, which investors will ask for.
No CAC payback period or how CAC is split by channel.
Unclear whether the price increase applies to existing bakeries or only new ones after the first year.

agenda.topic: Confirm current numbers and runway at today's burn (about 14 months)
Hiring now vs at $600k ARR: effect on runway and the November 20 board update
Modelling the $129 plan: churn sensitivity and payback
Series A story: which metrics to lead with, and what's missing
Next steps before the board update
